title: Hanukkah, eight lights
hookLine: eight nights of lights for the Temple's rededication; the odd part is that they go up, one more each night
tomorrow: the early church kept a martyr's death day as a birthday. why?

lines: OIL THAT SHOULD HAVE RUN OUT.
cards: Across the street, a window holds a row of small flames. Two one night. Three the next.
Then four. It looks backwards at first. The story behind it is about a jar of oil that should have run out.

So shouldn't the lights get fewer, the way oil burns down? Two schools of teachers argued over the count, a long time ago, and the Talmud kept both sides. The answer is in the window across the street.
The lesson is in why families follow one side and not the other.

teach.h: ONE JAR OF OIL BURNS EIGHT DAYS.
teach.b: The Talmud tells the story in a few lines. When the Greeks entered the Temple in Jerusalem, they made its oils impure.
When the Hasmonean family won, they searched and found one small jar, still sealed by the high priest, enough to light the lamp for one day. It was all they had. They lit it anyway.
It burned for eight days. The next year, those days were set as a festival of praise and thanks.
Hanukkah means dedication: the Temple given back to its purpose. Then the argument.
The house of Shammai said: light eight on the first night, then fewer, like the days still to come.

teach.h: IN HOLY THINGS, YOU GO UP.
teach.b: The house of Hillel said: light one, then add, because in holy things you go up, not down. Jewish practice follows Hillel.
That's why the menorah grows from one light to eight, and why the Talmud asks for it at the door, facing the street, so the miracle is made known.
One surprise for a friend tonight: the Gospel of John mentions this festival too. "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." The teaching underneath is Hillel's.
Holiness is something you climb. You don't start with a blaze and watch it shrink. You start with one small light, and each night you add one.

how: Jewish families light the menorah for the eight nights of Hanukkah, one more light each night, with blessings, often in a window or by the door so it can be seen from outside.

o: a harvest feast when families eat outdoors in huts
dedication: eight nights of lights, adding one each night
a fast of eight days before the Jewish new year begins

games.q: the lights and the argument: tap the pairs.
p: enough oil for one day, burned eight
start with eight, light fewer each night
start with one, add one each night
so the miracle is made known

s: Jewish practice lights all eight candles on the first night, then fewer
that was Shammai's view. Practice follows Hillel: one light, then one more each night.
the Gospel of John mentions the feast of the dedication
John 10:22: "the feast of the dedication, and it was winter."
the Talmud wants the lights kept inside, out of sight
it asks for the lamp at the door, facing the street, so the miracle is made known.

games.q: first night at a friend's Hanukkah. their kid wants to light all eight "to make it bigger." what does the custom say?
o: one light tonight, one more each night: Hillel's rule of going up in holiness.
all eight tonight, then one fewer each night, as the oil runs down.
any number works; the count was never part of the story.
games.why: The fewer-each-night view was real: it was Shammai's. But Jewish practice follows Hillel, so the menorah grows from one light to eight.

practice: At dusk, or right now, light one candle, or picture one if you can't. Set it where you can see it from across the room.
Watch the flame for the whole sit, and let it be the first light of something you'll add to, one night at a time.

wordCard.voice: Hanukkah: dedication, eight nights of lights remembering the Temple given back, one more light each night.

orig.note: Hebrew: dedication. The Temple given back to its purpose.

carryVoice: Your line: eight nights. Hillel's rule is that in holy things you go up, not down. Day 1640.
